sections.name: Health Psychology
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes what happens when stress activates the sympathetic nervous system?
options: The parasympathetic system shuts down permanently.
Leptin levels rise and hunger disappears.
The body immediately returns to baseline.
Hormones like cortisol are released, which can lead to hypertension, headaches, and immunosuppression.
questions.exp: Stress → sympathetic nervous system → cortisol → hypertension, headaches, immunosuppression.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of eustress?
options: Being stuck in traffic every day
Preparing for a wedding you're excited about
questions.exp: Eustress = challenging but manageable "good" stress. The others are distress.

questions.stem: A dead phone, no Wi-Fi, and a deadline in the same afternoon are examples of:
questions.exp: Daily hassles are everyday distress.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of household dysfunction as an ACE?
options: Having a parent who is incarcerated
questions.exp: Household dysfunction: substance abuse, domestic violence, parent with mental illness, or an incarcerated parent.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why people with many ACEs face higher health risks as adults?
options: Stress during childhood affects how a child's brain and body develop, which shows up later in life.
ACEs only affect children until age 17.
ACEs are caused by genetic disorders.
ACEs make people less likely to smoke.
questions.exp: Your slide: ACEs affect a child's brain and health as they grow up, raising risks like heart disease and depression.

questions.stem: In which stage of the General Adaptation Syndrome is the body still in high stress, with cortisol and epinephrine flowing and reserves being used up?
questions.exp: Alarm = immediate fight-or-flight; resistance = sustained stress; exhaustion = depleted.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the tend-and-befriend theory?
options: People under stress avoid all social contact.
Under stress, some people, mainly women, respond by caring for others and building social connections instead of fight-or-flight.
Stress causes the body to become exhausted immediately.
questions.exp: It's part of evolutionary psychology: protecting offspring and building support.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the difference between problem-focused and emotion-focused coping?
options: Problem-focused coping changes the stressor itself; emotion-focused coping changes how you feel about it.
Emotion-focused coping deals with the root cause.
questions.exp: Problem-focused = fix the problem. Emotion-focused = regulate the feeling.

questions.stem: When is emotion-focused coping most likely to be used?
options: When the stressor can easily be changed
questions.exp: Problem-focused coping works best when the stressor can be changed or controlled.

sections.name: Intro to Psychological Disorders
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: According to your slides, professionals label thoughts, feelings, and behaviors as a disorder when they are:
questions.exp: The 3 Ds.

questions.stem: A man believes that wearing his lucky socks helps his team win, but he functions well and isn't bothered by it. Why is this NOT considered a disorder?
questions.exp: A disorder needs all 3 Ds, not just being unusual.

questions.stem: Which approach explains disorders through chemical imbalances, genetics, tumors, or brain structure?
questions.exp: Biological = medical/genetic issues and neurotransmitters/hormones.

questions.stem: Which approach explains disorders as responses learned through conditioning and reinforcement?
questions.exp: Behavioral = learned through the environment.

questions.stem: A therapist believes a client's anxiety comes from unconscious conflicts rooted in childhood. Which approach is this?
questions.exp: Psychodynamic = unconscious thoughts and childhood experiences.

questions.stem: Which approach says disorders result from a lack of social support and not being able to reach your full potential?
questions.exp: Humanistic = potential and support.

sections.name: Anxiety Disorders
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes anxiety disorders?
options: Extreme mood swings between mania and depression
Persistent, excessive worry and fear that significantly interfere with daily life
A loss of connection between thoughts and identity
questions.exp: That's the slide's definition; GAD, panic disorder, and phobias are examples.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a specific phobia?
options: Constant worry about many everyday things
An intense or irrational fear that is out of proportion to the actual threat
Sudden panic attacks for no reason
A fear of being judged in social situations
questions.exp: Specific phobias are tied to a particular object or situation.

questions.stem: Which disorder is described as "nonspecific worry and fear" lasting at least 6 months?
questions.exp: GAD worry isn't tied to one specific thing.

questions.stem: A key symptom of panic disorder is:
questions.exp: Panic disorder: panic attacks plus anxiety about having panic attacks.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a cognitive symptom of agoraphobia?
options: Intense fear of being trapped or unable to escape
questions.exp: Sweating, tremors, and rapid heartbeat are physical; staying home is behavioral.

questions.stem: A child becomes terrified of dogs after watching her mother scream every time a dog walks by. Which cause of anxiety disorders does this show?
questions.exp: Behavioral causes include modeling anxiety responses from others.

questions.stem: Which neurotransmitter imbalances do your slides link to anxiety disorders?
questions.exp: Biological cause: imbalances in serotonin and GABA, plus hormonal imbalances.

sections.name: Depressive & Bipolar Disorders
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes depressive disorders?
options: A temporary bad mood after a disappointment
Extreme mood swings between mania and depression
A sad, empty, or irritable mood with physical and cognitive changes that affect functioning
questions.exp: Depression is a mental health condition, not just a temporary mood swing.

questions.stem: What is the key time difference between major depressive disorder and persistent depressive disorder?
options: MDD lasts 2+ years; persistent lasts 2+ weeks
MDD lasts 2+ weeks; persistent depressive disorder lasts 2+ years
questions.exp: MDD = 2 weeks. Persistent = 2 years.

questions.stem: Changes in sleep in major depressive disorder can include:
questions.exp: Your slide: changes in sleep (insomnia or hypersomnia).

questions.stem: Why would someone with long-term depression who also has a manic episode NOT be diagnosed with persistent depressive disorder?
options: Manic episodes only happen in children
A manic episode means it would most likely be bipolar disorder
questions.exp: Persistent depressive disorder requires no manic episodes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a symptom of a manic episode?
options: Decreased need for sleep and racing thoughts
questions.exp: The other three are depressive-episode symptoms.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares Bipolar I and Bipolar II?
options: Bipolar I has full mania and can include psychosis; Bipolar II has hypomania and no psychosis.
Bipolar II is more severe than Bipolar I.
questions.exp: Bipolar II is less severe but more common.

questions.stem: Which neurotransmitters do your slides link to both depressive and bipolar disorders?
questions.exp: Both slides list imbalances in serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine.

questions.stem: Family histories and twin studies of depression suggest that:
options: Depression is caused only by stress
questions.exp: Your slide: family histories and twin studies indicate a genetic component.

sections.name: Neurodevelopmental Disorders
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes neurodevelopmental disorders?
options: Disorders that always start in adulthood
Issues in central nervous system functioning that begin to appear in early childhood
Disorders involving false beliefs and perceptions
questions.exp: They involve social, intellectual, academic, or interpersonal functioning.

questions.stem: ADHD is characterized by a persistent pattern of:
questions.exp: That pattern must interfere with functioning or development.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an inattention symptom of ADHD?
options: Often loses things and is easily distracted
questions.exp: Talking excessively and running are hyperactivity; blurting out is impulsivity.

questions.stem: For an ADHD diagnosis, several symptoms must be present:
options: Before age 12 and in two or more settings
questions.exp: Before 12, in 2+ settings, for 6+ months.

questions.stem: Why can it be difficult to diagnose ADHD in very young children?
options: Many ADHD symptoms also occur in children without ADHD
There is no test for ADHD in any age group
questions.exp: Average onset is around age 8; earlier, normal kid behavior looks similar.

questions.stem: Why is autism called a "spectrum" disorder?
options: Its symptoms range from mild to severe
questions.exp: Your slide: symptoms range from mild to severe.

questions.stem: ADHD and ASD both have high heritability. This means they:
options: Tend to run in families, suggesting a strong genetic component
questions.exp: Heritability = tends to run in families.

questions.stem: According to your slides, ASD is:
options: Over 3 times more common in boys than girls
Equally common in boys and girls
questions.exp: About 1 in 31 children aged 8; over 3 times more common in boys.

sections.name: Dissociative Disorders
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes dissociative disorders?
options: A loss of connection between thoughts, memories, feelings, surroundings, behavior, and identity
Extreme highs and lows in mood
questions.exp: They involve escaping from reality in unhealthy ways.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a symptom of dissociative amnesia?
options: Loss of autobiographical information, like personal identity or relationships
questions.exp: Dissociative amnesia = inability to recall important personal information.

questions.stem: The distinct personality states in dissociative identity disorder are called:
questions.exp: Each alter has its own identity, memories, behaviors, and perspectives.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of a fugue state?
options: A man feels sad for two weeks
A woman travels to another city and doesn't know who she is
A child is afraid of dogs
A student can't focus in class
questions.exp: Fugue: wandering or traveling without awareness of identity or situation.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes DID from schizophrenia?
options: DID involves multiple distinct identities; schizophrenia involves psychosis like delusions and hallucinations
DID is caused by too much dopamine
questions.exp: "Split personality" is DID, not schizophrenia.

sections.name: Schizophrenia Spectrum
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: To be diagnosed on the schizophrenia spectrum, a patient must have:
options: At least 2 symptoms for at least 6 months
questions.exp: Your slide: at least 2 symptoms (positive and negative) for at least 6 months.

questions.stem: Why did the DSM-5 place schizophrenia on a spectrum?
options: People experience its symptoms in a variety of ways
It is the same as bipolar disorder
It always has the same severity
questions.exp: It's a spectrum of psychotic disorders.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a positive symptom of schizophrenia?
questions.exp: Positive = added. The others are negative (absent).

questions.stem: A patient says, "The table sky running blue mustard because seven." This is an example of:
questions.exp: Stringing words together in an unusual way = word salad.

questions.stem: A man believes he is a famous king chosen to save the world. This is a:
questions.exp: Grandeur = false belief of importance.

questions.stem: According to the dopamine hypothesis, what causes the positive symptoms of schizophrenia?
questions.exp: This is also why antipsychotics block dopamine receptors.

questions.stem: Which of the following is listed on your slides as a cause of schizophrenia?
options: Prenatal exposure to viruses like flu, herpes, or rubella
questions.exp: Also genetics and imbalances in dopamine and glutamate.

questions.stem: The diathesis-stress model suggests that:
options: Genes alone always cause mental illness
Stress alone always causes mental illness
Mental illness only comes from childhood
Stress can trigger a genetic or biological predisposition to mental illness
questions.exp: Diathesis = predisposition; stress = the trigger.

sections.name: OCD & Trauma Disorders
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: In OCD, obsessions are best described as:
options: Repetitive behaviors the person feels driven to perform
questions.exp: Obsessions = thoughts; compulsions = actions.

questions.stem: Which sequence matches the OCD cycle?
questions.exp: The relief reinforces the compulsion, and the cycle repeats.

questions.stem: How did the DSM-5 change the classification of OCD?
options: It moved OCD and related disorders out of anxiety disorders into their own category
It removed OCD from the DSM
It made OCD a personality disorder
questions.exp: This showed they are distinct from anxiety disorders.

questions.stem: Which neurotransmitter is OCD linked to being too low?
questions.exp: Your slide: low serotonin plus imbalances in GABA and glutamate.

questions.stem: Which of the following is one of the DSM-5 criteria for hoarding disorder?
options: Persistent difficulty discarding possessions regardless of their actual value
questions.exp: Plus distress at discarding and clutter that compromises living areas.

questions.stem: PTSD, acute stress disorder, and adjustment disorders have similar symptoms but differ in:
questions.exp: All three result from exposure to a traumatic or stressful event.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a symptom of PTSD?
options: Hypervigilance, or always being on guard
questions.exp: Also intrusive thoughts, nightmares, flashbacks, anxiety, depression, and sleep problems.

sections.name: Feeding & Eating Disorders
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a primary symptom of anorexia nervosa?
options: Eating large amounts in two hours
Intense fear of gaining weight even though underweight
questions.exp: Anorexia also includes refusing to maintain a minimally normal weight.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes bulimia nervosa?
options: Refusing to eat and becoming severely underweight
Recurrent binge eating plus behaviors to prevent weight gain, like vomiting or laxatives
questions.exp: Binge + trying to prevent weight gain.

questions.stem: Why can bulimia nervosa be hard to spot?
options: People often binge and purge privately
People with bulimia are always underweight
questions.exp: Your slide: bulimia can be hard to spot because of private bingeing and purging.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a cognitive cause of eating disorders?
options: Dysfunctional attitudes about physical appearance and perfectionism
questions.exp: Family history is genetic; brain chemistry is biological; bullying is social.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a long-term risk of eating disorders, according to your slides?
options: Permanent harm to the heart, digestive system, bones, teeth, and mouth
questions.exp: They're also linked with depression, anxiety, self-harm, and suicidal thoughts.

sections.name: Personality Disorders
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes personality disorders?
options: Brief reactions to a stressful event
Enduring, inflexible patterns of experience and behavior that deviate from one's culture and begin in adolescence or early adulthood
Disorders that always begin in early childhood
questions.exp: They're stable over time and must interfere with daily living.

questions.stem: Which cluster is described as dramatic, emotional, and erratic?
questions.exp: Cluster B: antisocial, histrionic, narcissistic, borderline.

questions.stem: Which personality disorder belongs in Cluster C?
questions.exp: Cluster C: avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive.

questions.stem: A woman constantly needs to be the center of attention and makes dramatic, theatrical displays to get it. Which disorder fits best?
questions.exp: Histrionic = excessive emotionality and attention-seeking.

questions.stem: A man has an intense fear of rejection and avoids relationships, even though he wants friends. Which disorder fits best?
questions.exp: Schizoid people lack interest in relationships; avoidant people fear rejection.

questions.stem: Which disorder involves instability in mood, self-image, and relationships, with intense emotions and impulsivity?
questions.exp: DBT was originally developed to treat borderline personality disorder.

questions.stem: A woman believes in magic, dresses very oddly, and is suspicious of others. Which disorder fits best?
questions.exp: Schizotypal: odd behavior and appearance, magical thinking.

questions.stem: A manager refuses to let anyone else do tasks because "they won't do it right," and is rigid about rules and order. Which disorder fits best?
questions.exp: OCPD: perfectionism, rigidity, control, can't delegate.

questions.stem: Which of the following is listed as an environmental cause of personality disorders?
options: Early childhood abuse, neglect, or trauma and poor attachment
questions.exp: Brain differences are biological; parenting styles are cultural; predisposition is genetic.

sections.name: Treatment
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes deinstitutionalization?
options: The late 20th-century movement to close asylums and treat patients with medication and therapy as outpatients
questions.exp: New medications made outpatient treatment possible.

questions.stem: Who can prescribe psychotropic medications?
questions.exp: Most psychotherapy is done by clinical psychologists and psychotherapists, who can't prescribe.

questions.stem: A therapist combines cognitive techniques with medication and group work to fit one client's needs. This is:
questions.exp: Eclectic = combining methods from different approaches.

questions.stem: Which statement about psychotropic medications is correct?
options: They treat symptoms, not the underlying cause of the disorder
They are never used with psychotherapy
questions.exp: Your slide: they treat symptoms by interacting with neurotransmitters.

questions.stem: Anti-anxiety medications like Xanax and Valium work by:
questions.exp: They're benzodiazepines that depress the CNS.

questions.stem: A patient taking an antipsychotic develops repetitive, involuntary movements. This side effect is:
questions.exp: Tardive dyskinesia is a medication-induced movement disorder.

questions.stem: Which treatment uses magnetic pulses to treat chronic depression with no seizures and no memory loss?
questions.exp: ECT causes a seizure and can cause memory loss.

questions.stem: Which is a drawback of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)?
options: It requires surgery on the frontal lobe
Memory loss and a 40% relapse rate within 6 months
questions.exp: ECT is used for extreme depression and reduces suicide risk, but no one knows why it works.

questions.stem: The cardinal rule of psychotherapy is that a therapist must keep information confidential unless:
options: The patient is a danger to themselves or others
questions.exp: Confidentiality is broken only for danger to self or others.

questions.stem: What did Hans Eysenck's 1950s study conclude?
options: Psychotherapy, especially psychoanalysis, was no more effective than no treatment
Group therapy is better than individual therapy
questions.exp: Today, meta-analysis shows psychotherapy is effective, especially with medication.

questions.stem: Which ethical guideline means "do no harm" and weighing benefits against risks?
questions.exp: Justice = equal treatment; integrity = honesty; fidelity = trust and responsibility.

questions.stem: During free association, a patient suddenly goes blank and can't remember details. A psychodynamic therapist would call this:
questions.exp: Resistance is a mental block.

questions.stem: What does research show about hypnosis?
options: It is the main treatment for schizophrenia
It was invented by Carl Rogers
It is NOT a valid way to retrieve memories, but it is used today for pain and anxiety
questions.exp: Freud used it; research shows it doesn't retrieve memories accurately.

questions.stem: A therapist shows a caring, accepting, nonjudgmental attitude toward a client no matter what the client says. This is:
questions.exp: A key part of Carl Rogers' person-centered therapy.

questions.stem: Aaron Beck's negative cognitive triad involves negative thoughts about:
options: Yourself, the world, and the future
questions.exp: "I'm worthless," "No one cares," "Things will never get better."

questions.stem: A therapist helps a client with a fear of spiders rank situations from least to most scary while learning relaxation techniques. This is:
questions.exp: Fear hierarchy + relaxation = systematic desensitization.

questions.stem: Which therapy is described as the opposite of systematic desensitization?
questions.exp: Aversion therapy pairs an unpleasant state with an unwanted behavior.

questions.stem: A patient watches a screen showing her heart rate and learns to slow it down. This is:
questions.exp: Biofeedback: monitoring, feedback, learning.

questions.stem: Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) was originally developed to treat:
questions.exp: Its skills: mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of group therapy over individual therapy?
options: It's cheaper and shows people they aren't the only ones with the problem
questions.exp: Individual therapy is more personalized and flexible but expensive.

sections.name: Practice exam: Treatment & Personality
examTips: Like your test: 25 multiple-choice questions, mostly applied. Turn the Timer on and don't look anything up.
About 1 minute per question. Flag hard ones and come back.
tips: Every question gives a situation; name the treatment, drug, side effect, ethics principle or disorder that fits.
Wrong choices are close mix-ups (CBT vs. REBT, desensitization vs. aversion, schizoid vs. avoidant). Cross out what doesn't fit the details.

questions.stem: A man with schizophrenia starts a drug that quiets his hallucinations. Months later he develops repetitive, involuntary lip-smacking. Which drug type and side effect fit?
options: An anti-anxiety drug; dependency and drowsiness
questions.exp: Antipsychotics block dopamine to reduce positive symptoms; tardive dyskinesia is their movement side effect.
why: Tardive dyskinesia comes from antipsychotics, and SSRIs don't treat hallucinations.
Catatonic stupor is a negative symptom of schizophrenia, not a drug side effect.
Benzodiazepines can cause dependency, but they don't reduce hallucinations.

questions.stem: A patient is diagnosed with bipolar disorder. Which medication is the classic treatment on your slides?
options: Prozac, an SSRI that blocks serotonin reuptake
Xanax, a benzodiazepine that boosts GABA
Antabuse, which makes alcohol cause sickness
questions.exp: Mood stabilizers like lithium treat bipolar disorder.
why: SSRIs are antidepressants; the bipolar example is lithium.
That is an anti-anxiety drug.
Antabuse is used in aversion therapy for alcoholism.

questions.stem: A doctor prescribes a drug that depresses the central nervous system and increases the effects of GABA to calm a patient's constant tension. Which side effects should the patient watch for?
options: Memory loss and a 40% relapse rate
questions.exp: Anti-anxiety medications (benzodiazepines) can cause drowsiness and dependency.
why: Those are antipsychotic side effects.
Those are ECT drawbacks.
Those are listed for antidepressants (SSRIs).

questions.stem: A patient with chronic depression wants a brain-stimulation treatment where she stays awake, has no seizure, and has no memory loss. Which fits?
questions.exp: rTMS uses magnetic pulses: no seizures, no memory loss, person awake.
why: ECT causes a seizure and can cause memory loss.
That is psychosurgery and is rarely used today.
Biofeedback trains control of body responses; it doesn't stimulate the brain.

questions.stem: A family is considering ECT for their son's severe depression. Which concern is supported by your slides?
options: It cuts the main connections to the frontal lobe
It only reduces the positive symptoms of schizophrenia
It is mainly used for mild, everyday anxiety
questions.exp: ECT drawbacks: memory loss, about 40% relapse within 6 months, and no one knows why it works.
why: That describes a lobotomy.
ECT is used for extreme depression.
ECT is for extreme depression.

questions.stem: During a session, a client says he plans to seriously hurt his roommate tonight. What should the therapist do?
options: Keep it private, because confidentiality has no exceptions at all
Wait until the next session to discuss it further
Break confidentiality to protect the roommate
Switch the client to group therapy
questions.exp: Confidentiality is the cardinal rule unless the client is a danger to themselves or others.
why: The exception is danger to self or others.
The danger is immediate.
That doesn't address the danger.

questions.stem: A therapist tells a client a treatment is proven to work, even though she knows it isn't. Which ethics principle is she violating?
questions.exp: Integrity: honesty, accuracy and transparency. No lying to the client.
why: Justice is about fairness and equal access.
That is about weighing harm; the problem here is lying.
That is about privacy and self-determination.

questions.stem: A man cons elderly people out of their savings, lies constantly, and shows no guilt. Which disorder and cluster fit best?
questions.exp: Antisocial personality disorder: disregard for others' rights, no remorse. Cluster B.
why: Narcissism is in Cluster B, and its core is self-importance, not violating others' rights.
Paranoid personality disorder is distrust of others.
Schizotypal is Cluster A and involves odd thinking.

questions.stem: A therapist mostly listens, restates the client's feelings ("It sounds like you feel unseen"), and never tells him what to do. Which therapy and technique are these?
options: Psychodynamic therapy, using free association and dream interpretation
questions.exp: Rogers' person-centered therapy uses active listening: echo, restate, clarify.
why: The therapist isn't interpreting the unconscious.
CBT actively challenges thoughts.
REBT is confrontational, not non-directive.

questions.stem: A therapist bluntly tells an anxious client, "It's irrational to believe everyone must like you," then has him replace that belief. Which therapy is this?
questions.exp: REBT (Ellis) confronts irrational beliefs: identify, challenge, replace.
why: That is non-directive and accepting, not confrontational.
That uses relaxation and a fear hierarchy.
That explores the unconscious.

questions.stem: A client afraid of flying learns deep breathing, then imagines each step from booking a ticket to takeoff while staying calm. Which therapy is this?
questions.exp: Systematic desensitization: a fear hierarchy plus relaxation.
why: Aversion pairs an unwanted behavior with something unpleasant.
That rewards behavior with tokens.
REBT confronts beliefs; this uses relaxation and a fear hierarchy.

questions.stem: To stop drinking, a man takes a pill that makes him sick whenever he drinks alcohol. Which therapy is this, and how does it work?
options: Aversion therapy: drinking is paired with feeling ill
Systematic desensitization: drinking is paired with relaxation
Token economy: he earns rewards for staying sober
Biofeedback: sensors show his body's reaction
questions.exp: Antabuse pairs a negative outcome with a previously pleasant stimulus.
why: That reduces fear; it doesn't make drinking unpleasant.
No rewards are involved.
No sensors or feedback are involved.

questions.stem: On a psychiatric ward, patients earn points for showering and making their beds and trade them for TV time. Which principle is at work?
questions.exp: A token economy rewards desired behavior with tokens.
why: No unpleasant state is paired with a behavior.
That is a humanistic attitude, not a reward system.
That is a psychodynamic technique.

questions.stem: A woman with tension headaches watches a screen that shows her muscle tension and gradually learns to lower it on purpose. Which therapy is this?
questions.exp: Biofeedback: sensors feed body data back so you learn to control it.
why: rTMS stimulates neurons with magnets.
Hypnosis induces relaxation but doesn't use sensor feedback.
Exposure is facing what you avoid.

questions.stem: A client with borderline personality disorder learns mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness. Which therapy is this?
questions.exp: DBT, a modified CBT, was originally developed for borderline personality disorder.
why: REBT confronts irrational beliefs.
That explores the unconscious.
That pairs a behavior with discomfort.

questions.stem: During free association, a patient goes blank every time her mother comes up. What would a psychodynamic therapist call this?
questions.exp: Resistance is a mental block during free association.
why: Flat affect is a lack of emotional expression in schizophrenia.
That is the therapist's accepting attitude.
That is a lack of movement.

questions.stem: A client says, "I'm a failure, nobody cares about me, and it will never get better." Which theory explains this pattern, and what is it called?
options: Eysenck's finding that therapy doesn't work
questions.exp: Beck: negative thoughts about me, the world and the future.
why: That is a therapist's accepting attitude.
Eysenck studied therapy outcomes, not thought patterns.
That is psychodynamic.

questions.stem: A student cites a 1950s study claiming therapy is no better than no treatment. Which reply best fits current evidence?
options: Meta-analyses show it works, especially with medication
The study proved that only psychoanalysis is effective for most people
Modern research shows therapy works only without medication
Therapy works best when there is no therapeutic alliance
questions.exp: Eysenck's 1950s claim has been answered by meta-analyses showing therapy is effective.
why: Eysenck found psychoanalysis no better than nothing.
It works best with medication.
A strong alliance helps therapy work.

questions.stem: A psychologist teaches a client relaxation, challenges his negative thoughts, and refers him for medication. Which approach is this?
questions.exp: Eclectic = combining methods that fit the client.
why: She is actively directing treatment.
She isn't exploring the unconscious.
That is the historical closing of asylums.

questions.stem: A clinical psychologist believes her client needs an antidepressant. What should happen?
options: The psychologist prescribes it herself after a full evaluation
The client buys it without a prescription
A doctor or psychiatrist prescribes it
questions.exp: Medications can only be prescribed by a doctor or psychiatrist.
why: Only doctors and psychiatrists can prescribe.
It needs a doctor or psychiatrist.
Hypnosis doesn't replace medication.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of group therapy over individual therapy, according to your slides?
options: It's more personalized and more private than individual sessions
questions.exp: Group: cheaper, shows you aren't alone, coping skills together, relieves isolation.
why: That describes individual therapy.
That is individual therapy.
Some disorders need individual therapy.

questions.stem: Ben has no friends and says he doesn't want any; praise and criticism leave him unmoved. Ana has no friends but badly wants them and fears rejection. Which disorders fit?
questions.exp: Schizoid = no interest in relationships; avoidant = wants them but fears rejection.
why: This swaps them: avoidant people want relationships but fear rejection.
Ben shows no magical thinking, and Ana isn't clingy for decisions.
Neither relies on others to make decisions.

questions.stem: In the order listed, which clusters do paranoid, histrionic and dependent personality disorders belong to?
questions.exp: A = odd (paranoid), B = dramatic (histrionic), C = anxious (dependent).
why: Paranoid is Cluster A, histrionic is Cluster B.
Histrionic is B and dependent is C.
Paranoid is A and dependent is C.

questions.stem: Kara has unstable moods, a shifting self-image, and intense, stormy relationships. Which disorder fits, and which therapy was first developed for it?
questions.exp: Borderline: instability in mood, self-image and relationships. DBT was developed for it.
why: Bipolar centers on mood episodes, not unstable relationships and self-image.
Histrionic is attention-seeking; REBT is mainly for anxiety.
Narcissism is grandiosity and entitlement.

questions.stem: Mark redoes all group work himself because no one else will do it right and keeps strict rules for everything, but he has no intrusive thoughts or rituals. Which fits best?
options: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) with obsessions and compulsions
questions.exp: OCPD: perfectionism, rigidity, need for control, can't delegate.
why: He has no intrusive thoughts or rituals.
He takes control instead of relying on others.
His issue is perfectionism, not distrust.
